author: angela-bouma
description: Full moon, bite, silver bullet: the movie werewolf is a recent invention. The oldest stories tell of a king punished by a god and a nobleman betrayed by his wife.

hero.hook: The fear is old. The monster changes its face with every age.

blocks.text: A full moon, a man sprouting fur and hunting by night, driven by a hunger he cannot control. To become a **werewolf**, you have to be bitten by another one, in some stories only under a full moon. Everyone knows this picture. It is also very recent.

The original story is far stranger. One of the earliest surviving accounts comes from the Greek historian [[Herodotus]], writing in the **5th century** BC. He describes the [[Neuri]], a people living north of the **Black Sea**: each of them, he was told, turns into a wolf for a few days every year before returning to human form. Herodotus records the story, but makes clear he does not believe a word of it.

The story most often linked to the werewolf is that of [[Lycaon]], king of [[Arcadia]], in Greece, as the Roman poet Ovid tells it in the *Metamorphoses*. **Jupiter**, king of the gods, visits Arcadia disguised as an ordinary traveler. Lycaon suspects his guest might be a god and decides to test him: he kills a hostage, cooks the body and serves it at the table. If the stranger is truly divine, he will know what he is eating.

blocks.caption: Lycaon flees the banquet and turns into a wolf before Jupiter's eyes. Engraving by Hendrick Goltzius, 1589.

blocks.text: Jupiter discovers the crime and punishes the king: he turns him into a wolf. His cruelty is finally given a shape to match. This is one of the oldest werewolf stories, and it looks nothing like ours. Lycaon is not bitten. No full moon, no silver. He becomes a wolf because **a god punishes him**.
The English exclamation "By Jove!" is at least 450 years old: the earliest recorded example appears in a play from 1575. "Jove" is the old name for Jupiter.

sections.title: Lycaon, the king turned into a wolf

blocks.text: Other ancient writers describe a less permanent transformation. A man could live for **nine or ten years** as a wolf, depending on who tells it, and then become human again, on one condition: he must never have tasted human flesh. [[Pliny the Elder]], a Roman naturalist of the 1st century, tells of a certain **Demaenetus** who goes through this. No monthly change, no full moon: a long exile, with the possibility of coming home.

These are literary accounts, not proof that anyone really spent **nine years** as a wolf. They deserve the same distance Herodotus kept from the Neuri, centuries earlier. The real historical fact lies elsewhere: not that it happened, but that ancient writers, generation after generation, kept telling each other that it did.

sections.title: Nine years in a wolf's skin

blocks.text: In the **12th century**, the poet [[Marie de France]] wrote one of the best-known werewolf stories of all: [[Bisclavret]]. Its hero is a nobleman who regularly turns into a wolf. His wife discovers the secret and eventually steals the clothes he needs to return to human form. Without them, he stays trapped in his wolf's skin.

blocks.caption: Marie de France at work, 13th-century illumination (BnF, Arsenal 3142).

blocks.text: There is something unusual about this werewolf: he is **not really a monster**. Bisclavret keeps his intelligence and his decency in the shape of the beast. The story is less about hunting a monster than about identity, marriage and betrayal. Appearances are misleading: a man who looks like a wolf can behave honorably, and an ordinary-looking human can behave cruelly.

The werewolf changes because the fears around it change. Ancient Greece punishes Lycaon with a god's curse. Medieval France asks what makes someone a monster at all. Early modern Europe folds him into **witchcraft** and the fear of the devil: the same era that produces its accused witches and its blood-drinking vampires.

blocks.caption: "The Werewolf" by Lucas Cranach the Elder, around 1512: a man on all fours attacks a village.

blocks.text: Hollywood finally gives him the **full moon** and the **silver bullet**. This is no longer a religious fear but a story built for the screen and sold as entertainment. So the werewolf has neither one shape nor one origin. Like the witch and the vampire, he is proof that every age invents the fear it needs, and then tells itself a story about it.

blocks.text: From the king punished by Jupiter to the movie monster, the werewolf has not one origin but many: every age lends it the fear it needs to tell.
